title: ALPS-HCC Score: A Dynamic Liver Stiffness Measurement-Based Machine Learning Model to Predict Risk of Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMS: Existing hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk scores specific to chronic hepatitis B (CHB) mostly rely solely on baseline indicators, limiting their applicability in clinical practice. By incorporating dynamic and static indicators, this study aimed to address this limitation by developing a machine learning (ML) model for HCC prediction in patients with CHB and compensated advanced chronic liver disease (cACLD). METHODS: ML models were trained to predict HCC in 1 272 patients with CHB and cACLD, who underwent at least 2 measurements from different centres and were further tested with external cohorts (n = 601). The first and last liver stiffness measurements were defined as the baseline and follow-up values, respectively. RESULTS: A total of 1 873 individuals with CHB and cACLD were included, with 192 patients (10.3%) developing HCC after a median of 30.7 months. Based on LASSO logistic regression, baseline age, baseline albumin concentration, follow-up albumin concentration, follow-up platelet count, and change in the liver stiffness measurement (∆LSM) were selected, with ∆LSM identified as the most important indicator. Developed using XGBoost, the ALPS-HCC score achieved the highest integrated AUROC (0.852), Harrell's C-index (0.852), and F1 score (0.944), and performed significantly better than existing HCC risk scores. Based on these results, our risk stratification performed well in terms of prognosis in the validation cohort, including the identification of low-risk (n = 250; reference), intermediate-risk (n = 91; hazard ratio [HR] = 5.25), and high-risk (n = 41; HR = 24.47) groups. CONCLUSIONS: ALPS-HCC score provides robust predictive power and screening capability for predicting HCC risk in patients with CHB and cACLD.

METHODS: ML models were trained to predict HCC in 1 272 patients with CHB and cACLD, who underwent at least 2 measurements from different centres and were further tested with external cohorts (n = 601). The first and last liver stiffness measurements were defined as the baseline and follow-up values, respectively. RESULTS: A total of 1 873 individuals with CHB and cACLD were included, with 192 patients (10.3%) developing HCC after a median of 30.7 months. Based on LASSO logistic regression, baseline age, baseline albumin concentration, follow-up albumin concentration, follow-up platelet count, and change in the liver stiffness measurement (∆LSM) were selected, with ∆LSM identified as the most important indicator. Developed using XGBoost, the ALPS-HCC score achieved the highest integrated AUROC (0.852), Harrell's C-index (0.852), and F1 score (0.944), and performed significantly better than existing HCC risk scores. Based on these results, our risk stratification performed well in terms of prognosis in the validation cohort, including the identification of low-risk (n = 250; reference), intermediate-risk (n = 91; hazard ratio [HR] = 5.25), and high-risk (n = 41; HR = 24.47) groups. CONCLUSIONS: ALPS-HCC score provides robust predictive power and screening capability for predicting HCC risk in patients with CHB and cACLD.

title: The HBV basal core promoter mutation confers a replicative advantage and transcriptionally reprograms hepatocytes toward HCC subtypes
abstract: Background: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) basal core promoter (BCP) and precore (PC) mutations occur during chronic HBV infection with the BCP-mutant being associated with increased hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) risk. Objectives: The effects of these mutants on viral replication, hepatocyte biology, and carcinogenesis remain poorly defined. To address this, we characterized BCP- and PC-mutants using human hepatocyte chimeric mice and asked whether the resulting infection-induced transcriptomes correspond to subsets of human HBV-related hepatocellular carcinomas (HBV-HCCs). Design: Isogenic wild-type (WT), BCP- and PC-mutants of HBV genotypes A, C, and D (HBV-A, -C, -D) were generated from recombinant covalently-closed circular DNA to infect chimeric mice. HBV-HCC transcriptomic datasets from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) were used to stratify association of HBV variants with HCC subtypes. Results: WT, BCP-mutant, and PC-mutant HBV sequences remained genetically stable. The BCP mutation, but not the PC mutation, accelerated the rise in serum viremia in HBV-D- and HBV-A-infected chimeras; in HBV-C, acceleration required both (PC+BCP) mutations. Further comparisons of HBV-D variants revealed that the BCP-mutant increased intrahepatic viral DNA, viral protein expression, and upregulated cancer-related pathways, including transcripts associated with a subset of HBV-HCCs. Analysis of HBV-HCC samples from the TCGA revealed that tumors often harbor a mixture of WT and mutant transcripts, and that WT- and BCP-mutant-associated HCCs exhibit distinct transcriptional profiles. Conclusions: The HBV BCP-mutant directly perturbs hepatocyte homeostasis via virus-intrinsic mechanisms, selectively activating cancer-related pathways and defining a molecularly distinct subset of HBV-HCC. These findings suggest that HBV variants form distinct subcategories of HBV-HCCs.

title: Combined RNA- and DNA-targeting CRISPR ribonucleoproteins enhance suppression of HBV transcripts
abstract: Introduction Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health problem and there is no curative treatment currently available. RNA-targeting CRISPR systems offer a potential alternative to DNA-editing nucleases by enabling direct degradation of viral transcripts without introducing genomic breaks. In this report, we evaluated the antiviral activity of synthetic guide RNA (gRNA)/Cas13d ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) targeting HBV RNA and a combination use with DNA-targeting RNPs. Methods We designed 10 gRNAs targeting conserved regions across the HBV transcriptome followed by screening for best candidate gRNA for Cas13d. To enhance antiviral efficacy, we evaluated multiplex RNA targeting using combined gRNA6+gRNA7/Cas13d RNPs, and combined RNA-targeting gRNA7/Cas13d with previously validated HBV DNA-targeting gRNA9/Cas9 and gRNA4/Cas12a RNPs for HBV treatment. Results Amongst these 10 gRNAs, gRNA7/Cas13d exhibited selective knockdown of its specific target RNA transcript without inducing a broad suppression of total HBV DNA, mRNAs, and proteins. The antiviral effect of gRNA7/Cas13d RNP was transient, diminishing by Day 3 post the treatment. The combined gRNA6+gRNA7/Cas13d treatment also did not further induce global HBV suppression compared with single gRNAs, although gRNA7/Cas13d still showed a robust target-specific RNA cleavage during the combined treatment in HBV cellular models. While gRNA9/Cas9 and gRNA4/Cas12a exhibited the dominant antiviral effects, either alone or in combination, leading to substantial reductions in HBV replication and expression, the addition of gRNA7/Cas13d further enhanced the suppression of the gRNA7-specific HBV RNA transcript, achieving up to an 80% reduction in the target RNA level. Discussion Collectively, these findings demonstrate that gRNA7/Cas13d can mediate target-specific HBV RNA cleavage but has limited overall antiviral activity when used alone as a single-agent; however, the combination of DNA- and RNA-targeting CRISPR-RNPs may provide a complementary approach for enhancing target-specific HBV RNA suppression.

title: Microelimination of hepatitis C in dialysis units: results from the Brazilian Registry for the elimination of HCV.
abstract: Introduction Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remains a major public health challenge, particularly among patients undergoing dialysis, who are disproportionately vulnerable and at increased risk of transmission. Micro-elimination strategies targeting high-risk subpopulations are a critical component for achieving the World Health Organization global HCV elimination goals. Methods This national, multicenter, prospective implementation study was conducted within the framework of the Brazilian Registry for the Elimination of HCV in Dialysis Units. All 904 active dialysis units in the country were invited; 384 (42.5%) joined voluntarily, and, within each, all eligible patients were enrolled (census) between 2021 and 2024. The HCV cascade of care was evaluated, including serological screening (anti-HCV), virological confirmation (HCV-RNA), treatment with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs), and assessment of sustained virologic response (SVR). Results A total of 66,601 patients were evaluated, yielding a national anti-HCV prevalence of 2.08%. HCV-RNA testing coverage reached 65.4%, with a positivity rate of 64.2% among those tested, resulting in an adjusted prevalence of active viremia of 1.34%. Among patients with detectable viremia, 74.2% initiated antiviral therapy, 92.6% completed treatment, and 93.3% achieved SVR. The main barriers identified along the cascade of care included limited availability of diagnostic tests and patient mortality. Discussion These findings indicate that Brazil has achieved robust therapeutic effectiveness indicators, placing the country at an advanced stage toward HCV elimination within the dialysis population. Nonetheless, important operational gaps persist, particularly in diagnostic confirmation. Conclusion Elimination of HCV in dialysis units is an achievable goal in Brazil. Sustained success depends on maintaining universal screening, ensuring prompt treatment initiation for confirmed cases, and strengthening continuous integration between services.

source_records.title: Microelimination of hepatitis C in dialysis units: results from the Brazilian Registry for the elimination of HCV.
source_records.abstract: Introduction Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection remains a major public health challenge, particularly among patients undergoing dialysis, who are disproportionately vulnerable and at increased risk of transmission. Micro-elimination strategies targeting high-risk subpopulations are a critical component for achieving the World Health Organization global HCV elimination goals. Methods This national, multicenter, prospective implementation study was conducted within the framework of the Brazilian Registry for the Elimination of HCV in Dialysis Units. All 904 active dialysis units in the country were invited; 384 (42.5%) joined voluntarily, and, within each, all eligible patients were enrolled (census) between 2021 and 2024. The HCV cascade of care was evaluated, including serological screening (anti-HCV), virological confirmation (HCV-RNA), treatment with direct-acting antivirals (DAAs), and assessment of sustained virologic response (SVR). Results A total of 66,601 patients were evaluated, yielding a national anti-HCV prevalence of 2.08%. Among patients with detectable viremia, 74.2% initiated antiviral therapy, 92.6% completed treatment, and 93.3% achieved SVR. The main barriers identified along the cascade of care included limited availability of diagnostic tests and patient mortality. Discussion These findings indicate that Brazil has achieved robust therapeutic effectiveness indicators, placing the country at an advanced stage toward HCV elimination within the dialysis population. Nonetheless, important operational gaps persist, particularly in diagnostic confirmation. Conclusion Elimination of HCV in dialysis units is an achievable goal in Brazil. Sustained success depends on maintaining universal screening, ensuring prompt treatment initiation for confirmed cases, and strengthening continuous integration between services.

title: Vaccination gaps and infection risk at dialysis initiation.
abstract: In this editorial, we comment on the study by Puri et al published in the World Journal of Nephrology, which highlights a neglected gap in preventive care at dialysis initiation: Inadequate protection against vaccine-preventable and endemic infections in advanced chronic kidney disease. In an incident hemodialysis cohort from a tertiary centre in North India, the authors report major deficiencies in adult vaccination against hepatitis B virus, pneumococcus, and influenza at dialysis entry, with more than half of patients having received none of the recommended immunizations. Concurrently, a substantial burden of tuberculosis - predominantly extrapulmonary - was observed, underscoring a dual infectious vulnerability at the outset of renal replacement therapy in endemic, resource-constrained settings. Importantly, vaccination uptake aligned with markers of health-system engagement rather than patient characteristics or presumed biological limitations: Prior nephrology follow-up and structured pre-transplant evaluation were associated with higher vaccination rates and indicators of anticipatory care, including permanent vascular access. These findings suggest that impaired immunogenicity may not be the sole barrier to vaccination in advanced kidney disease and are consistent with an association between delayed referral, fragmented care pathways, and avoidable infectious risk. Although limited by its single-centre, cross-sectional design, this study supports viewing dialysis initiation as a sentinel checkpoint for infection prevention. We argue for integrating vaccination assessment, delivery, serologic monitoring, and tuberculosis screening into pre-dialysis and dialysis-start workflows to operationalize preventive nephrology in routine practice.

title: Editorial: Community series in novel preclinical model, biomarker, treatment and drug delivery to address immune evasion in cancer, volume II
abstract: Cancer diagnosis remains challenging, largely because few biomarkers are sufficiently sensitive and specific for early detection. Tumour-immune crosstalk adds further complexity, making consistent early-stage detection difficult [1,2,3]. Without dependable biomarkers to guide clinical decisions, treatment outcomes can be inconsistent [4]. Building on our previous editorial [5], we have learned much about immune-cell-driven anti-tumour immunity and how tumours evade these immune responses, alongside promising biomarkers and treatment strategies that target these pathways. In this volume, 16 research groups contribute new work advancing this complex field.Progress in understanding cancer immune evasion is often held back by the limitations of existing laboratory model systems. Yang G et al (2026) addressed this gap by building an integrated preclinical platform for bladder cancer, combining genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs), single-cell RNA sequencing and organoid technology. This work delivers scalable, clinically relevant tools that can be used both to unpack immune-evasion mechanisms and test how well candidate drugs perform. Using another barcoded Kras G12D and Trp53-deficient mouse lung adenocarcinoma organoids from the same group (Chen W et al 2026), we also see how these combined approaches can drive biomarker discovery. Collectively, these findings highlight how GEMMs, organoid culture and single-cell sequencing together can reshape how we study tumour immune escape.Many manuscripts in this collection report new cancer biomarkers ranging from molecular signatures, microbial profiling to new blood-derived indices. From multiple myeloma, Tan J et al (2025) identified protein-tyrosine-phosphatase receptor gamma (PTPRG) as an important mediator of drug resistance and poor patient prognosis. Using single-cell transcriptomics and functional in-vitro experiments, the group showed that the malignant plasma-cell sub-cluster MalPlasma3, marked by high PTPRG expression, displays stem-like properties and high proliferative potential. This nominates PTPRG both as a prognostic biomarker and a potential therapeutic target for multiple myeloma. For pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) Wang E et al (2024) observed clear differences in biliary microbiota between patients and control participants. The Muribaculum strongly correlated with phosphatidic acid (10:0/a-17:0) and raised CA19-9 levels, a standard clinical tumour marker for PDAC. Their work suggests profiling biliary microbiota could offer a new predictive biomarker for this disease.Looking at bladder cancer, Yang J et al (2026) used combined bulk and single-cell RNA-sequencing data to pinpoint succinylation-associated genes, namely KCTD16, CD3D, and GSDMB, and described their roles in bladder-cancer immune evasion. In melanoma, Fan Y et al (2025) leveraged machine learning together with single-cell and bulk RNA-sequencing datasets to generate a Treg-based gene signature (Treg.Sig) that can predict how patients may respond to immune-checkpoint inhibitors. Meanwhile, Wang LP et al (2026) proposed adoptively transferred innate lymphoid cells type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s)could identify glioblastoma in vivo, indicating the possible role of ILC2 in glioblastoma, the most aggressive primary brain tumours.Moving to readily available clinical blood markers, Shi L et al (2026) found that higher pre-treatment neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR) were associated with. advanced-stage neuroblastoma. A combined NLR-PLR score performed better for risk stratification than either marker alone, though large-scale phase III trials are still needed for formal clinical validation.Beyond biomarker identification, several studies also shed light on underlying tumour-microenvironment mechanisms that drive immune escape. Wu F et al (2026) described how increased extracellular-matrix (ECM) stiffness creates an immunosuppressive tumour niche. High ECM stiffness impairs T-cell and natural-killer-cell activity, favours Treg and M2-macrophage differentiation, and supports YAP/TAZ-driven expansion of plasmacytoid dendritic cells. These effects are further amplified when cancer-associated fibroblasts become activated and trigger epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). In similar context, Chen H et al (2026) studyshowed that epigenetic dysregulation fuels nasopharyngeal carcinoma progression through EMT signalling, further disturbs the tumour microenvironment, enables immune evasion and contributes to treatment failure. This special issue also features a broad range of preclinical findings, clinical observations, meta-analyses and reviews focused on new therapeutic approaches and improved drug delivery. Starting with pre-clinical target work for papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), Lv Y et al (2026) identified plectin (PLEC) as a promising therapeutic target. Few actionable vulnerabilities are known for PTC, but the team validated PLEC function both in-vitro and in-vivo, and provided evidence that troglitazone may exert anti-tumour activity against PTC via PLEC-related pathways. For colorectal cancer, Qiu Z et al (2025) explored cell-membrane-coated nanoparticles as a drug-delivery platform. Combining these nanoparticles with conventional chemotherapy or targeted agents may improve tumour specificity and overall treatment efficacy. In addition, Wang C et al (2026)carried out a meta-analysis covering 26 studies and reported improved clinical outcomes for patients with advanced solid tumours treated with the tyrosine-kinase inhibitor anlotinib together with PD-L1 immune-checkpoint inhibitors. Meanwhile, He Y et al (2026) reviewed ongoing debates around managing human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal carcinoma. They argue that modern treatment planning should integrate immunological and genomic data to build personalised regimens, with the goal of maximising patient survival while minimising avoidable treatment toxicity.A descriptive case report by Xu B et al (2025) offered encouraging real-world clinical observations. A patient with decompensated hepatitis-B-related cirrhosis, advanced hepatocellular carcinoma and lung metastases achieved complete remission after three drug-eluting bead transarterial chemoembolization (DEB-TACE) sessions, followed by 14 weeks of lenvatinib and 5 months of camrelizumab. No tumour recurrence was seen over 10 months of follow-up. Even so, larger formal studies are required to confirm these promising results. Meanwhile, in the vaccine space, Gao C et al (2025) analysed 442 clinical trials investigating melanoma vaccines. While combining melanoma vaccines with immune-checkpoint inhibitors holds clear therapeutic promise, many candidate approaches fail to progress to phase III trials, leaving high-level clinical evidence limited.Taken together, the work assembled in this Research Topic highlights how advances in pre-clinical platforms, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic development work hand-in-hand to unpack cancer immune evasion. Improved model systems such as genetically engineered mouse models paired with organoid and single-cell sequencing technologies not only help us trace the mechanisms behind tumour immune escape but also serve as critical test-beds for identifying and validating new candidate biomarkers. From molecular signatures and microbial markers to readily accessible haematological indices, these biomarkers hold real potential to refine risk stratification, predict treatment response, and guide patient-specific clinical decisions.Moving from bench toward bedside, the collection also underscores encouraging therapeutic strategies ranging from novel drug targets and smart nanoparticle-based delivery systems to combination immunotherapies, paving new path for cancer clinics. Nevertheless, many of these promising findings are still rooted in pre-clinical observations, small-scale studies or retrospective analyses. Several candidate approaches have yet to complete large-scale phase III evaluation, creating a well-recognised translational gap between laboratory discovery and routine patient care.To bridge this gap, coordinated, multi-disciplinary and multi-centre trials, supported by thoughtful policy and optimised clinical study design, will be essential. As a collective, these 16 contributions reinforce that no single solution can overcome cancer immune evasion. Instead, sustained progress depends on integrating better pre-clinical tools, robust biomarkers, innovative treatment and drug-delivery approaches. We hope the findings presented in this volume will stimulate further research, spark cross-group collaboration, and ultimately bring tangible clinical benefit for patients facing immune-evading cancers.

title: Linking Military Blast Exposure to Veterans Health Administration Diagnoses: Chronic Health Outcomes in the Millennium Cohort Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES To examine associations between high-level blast (HLB) exposure and occupational risk for low-level blast (LLB) exposure during military service and subsequent chronic medical diagnoses among US Veterans receiving Veterans Health Administration (VHA) care. METHODS The Millennium Cohort Study is a population-based cohort study of US service members and Veterans enrolled beginning in 2001 and followed with surveys every 3-5 years. Analyses included participants enrolled between 2001 and 2013 who completed the 2011-2013 survey, had separated from military service, had complete blast and covariate data, and used VHA care for at least 2 calendar years during follow-up. HLB was assessed by self-report of injury resulting from blast or explosion. LLB risk was classified using military occupational specialty codes. Incident VHA-documented diagnoses from 2013 to 2021 were analyzed using modified Poisson regression to estimate adjusted prevalence ratios (APRs) and 95% CIs. RESULTS Among N = 36,641 Veterans, HLB exposure was associated with increased likelihood of several VHA-documented incident diagnoses, including hepatitis B (APR [1.46]; 95% CI [1.13-1.89]), hepatitis C (1.89; [1.30-2.75]), diabetes (1.28; [1.07-1.52]), hypercholesterolemia (1.31; [1.18-1.46]), hyperlipidemia (1.12, [1.06-1.18]), obesity (1.07, [1.01-1.15]), seizures (1.79; [1.47-2.18]), angina (1.43; [1.18-1.73]), hypertension(1.08; [1.02-1.15]), other heart condition (1.15; [1.05-1.28]), stroke (1.35; [1.05-1.74]), chronic bronchitis (1.28; [1.07-1.52]), emphysema (1.26; [1.05-1.52]), sinusitis (1.13, [1.04-1.23]), neuropathy (1.38; [1.24-1.54]), and bladder infection (1.54; [1.14-2.08]). Occupational risk for LLB exposure was associated with lower likelihood of hepatitis C (0.67; [0.45-0.97]), diabetes (0.84; [0.72-0.99]), hyperlipidemia (0.94; [0.90-0.99]), sinusitis (0.91; [0.85-0.99]), and Crohn disease (0.62; [0.41-0.94]). A significant multiplicative interaction was observed for hepatitis B (1.92; [1.13-3.25]). Additive interaction estimates were generally subadditive, suggesting that high occupational risk for LLB attenuated rather than amplified the associations between HLB and most outcomes. DISCUSSION Among Veterans receiving VHA care, HLB exposure during military service was associated with a higher prevalence of several clinical conditions years after separation from service. These findings suggest that blast exposure represents a long-term occupational health risk with implications for neurologic disease burden and systemic health.

title: Progress Towards Eliminating Hepatitis C as a Public Health Threat in Norway.
abstract: The World Health Organisation aims to eliminate hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection as a public health threat by 2030. We assessed progress towards HCV elimination in Norway until the end of 2024. We used linked national registry data to describe diagnosed cases of HCV infection by treatment uptake and case characteristics, and the incidence of HCV-related death. We updated a stochastic compartmental model to estimate HCV incidence and prevalence among people who inject drugs and migrants. We summarised all available data to assess progress towards HCV elimination targets. Among 12,620 HCV RNA-positive cases still living in Norway in 2024, 10,824 (86%) had been treated. Among people who inject drugs the estimated incidence was 20 (95% credible interval (CrI): 8-39) new infections, or 0.3 per 100 (95% CrI: 0.1-0.5), and the estimated prevalence was 1498 (95% Crl, 549-3631) chronic infections in 2024. Among migrants, prevalence increased from 598 (95% CrI: 179-1156) in 2021 to 2228 (95% CrI: 1394-3071) in 2024. HCV-related deaths plateaued at 0.6-0.8 per 100,000 from 2017-2024. Norway achieved global targets for HCV incidence, mortality, treatment uptake, harm reduction and (likely) blood safety. There is a lack of data on the target for diagnostic coverage. We conclude that Norway has entered a new phase of the HCV epidemic, with low incidence of new infections, low mortality, and with prevalence becoming more influenced by patterns of migration. Further decentralisation and integration of testing and treatment are necessary to reach new national goals.

title: Community behavioural resilience and STIs: Predictors of pandemic preparedness in a low-resource setting in Cameroon.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) infect 374 million people annually, with sub-Saharan Africa bearing the highest burden. Community behavioural resilience remains poorly understood in low-income settings, creating a critical gap in STI pandemic preparedness. This study identifies predictors of willingness to adopt protective behaviours during a hypothetical STI outbreak in rural Cameroon. METHODS: We conducted a community-based survey in 2022 among residents of three riverine health areas in the Bafia Health District, Cameroon. Participants (N=372; 202 females [54.3%], 170 males [45.7%]) ≥18 y of age were enrolled; 336 with complete data were included in regression analyses. All participants were assessed for STI knowledge (awareness of 10 pathogens), self-reported STI history, current symptoms, willingness to undertake STI screening and willingness to abstain from sexual intercourse in a hypothetical STI pandemic scenario. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors of willingness to abstain. RESULTS: Among 336 participants, 247 (73.5%) reported a willingness to abstain from sexual intercourse during a hypothetical STI pandemic. The strongest independent predictors of protective intention were willingness to undertake STI screening (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 10.3 [95% confidence interval {CI} 4.55 to 24.2], p<0.001) and self-reported history of an STI (aOR 4.88 [95% CI 2.16 to 11.5], p<0.001). Knowledge of Chlamydia trachomatis (aOR 3.91 [95% CI 1.16 to 13.0], p=0.026) and hepatitis B (aOR 3.50 [95% CI 1.55 to 8.02], p=0.003), as well as age 30-39 y (aOR 5.94 [95% CI 1.51 to 28.3], p=0.016), were also significant predictors. In this study, a low overall STI knowledge score was paradoxically associated with higher odds of protective intention (aOR 10.7 [95% CI 1.57 to 76.7], p=0.016). The wide CI reflects statistical instability from small cell counts, thus the estimates should be regarded as exploratory. CONCLUSIONS: Community behavioural intentions during a hypothetical STI pandemic are driven more by experiential factors (personal STI history and willingness to seek testing) than by general STI knowledge. These findings are based on stated behavioural intentions in a hypothetical scenario, not observed behaviour. Still, the implication is clear. Pandemic preparedness policies must therefore integrate experiential drivers, including routine asymptomatic screening and accessible diagnostic services, to strengthen community behavioural resilience. This experience-aware model offers scalable insights for low- and middle-income countries and global health security planning.

title: Prognostic Value of Liver Stiffness in Advanced Chronic Liver Disease After Hepatitis C Virus Eradication.
abstract: Background & aim Sustained-virological-response (SVR) after direct-acting-antiviral (DAA) therapy improves outcomes in patients with HCV-related compensated-advanced-chronic-liver-disease (cACLD). However, it remains unclear whether absolute post-SVR LSM or LSM reduction better predicts prognosis after SVR. This study evaluated the prognostic performance of absolute-values-LSM versus dynamic-change for predicting liver-related-events after SVR. Methods We retrospectively analysed patients with HCV-related cACLD treated with DAA between December 2014 and March 2022. Baseline and post-SVR non-invasive tests (LSM, FIB-4 and APRI) were assessed. Predictive performance for liver-related events was evaluated using time-dependent receiver operating characteristic analysis. Associations between Baveno-VII criteria for clinically significant LSM improvement and clinical outcomes were assessed using Fine-Grey competing-risk models. Results During a median of 60 months (95%; CI 52-69), 11/135 patients (8%) developed liver-related events. Patients who developed events had higher baseline LSM than those who remained event-free (24 vs. 18 kPa, p = 0.049), and higher follow-up LSM values (20 vs. Follow-up LSM showed good discriminative ability for liver-related events within the first 3 years after SVR (tAUC at 2 years: 0.86 [95% CI 0.75-0.97]; tAUC at 3 years: 0.82 [0.71-0.93]). Follow-up LSM was significantly superior to ΔLSM and percentage ΔLSM at both 2 and 3 years (all p ≤ 0.028). In competing-risk analysis, only follow-up LSM > 20 kPa was significantly associated with liver-related events (subdistribution hazard ratio 5.61, p = 0.007), whereas Baveno-VII criteria for LSM regression were not (SHR 0.33, p = 0.097). Conclusions Absolute post-treatment-LSM provides stronger prognostic information than dynamic changes from baseline. These findings support repeated post-SVR LSM assessment for risk stratification suggesting the relevance of residual liver disease in predicting liver-related outcomes.

title: 特別な誘因なく自然経過でB型肝炎ウイルスの再活性化(de novo B型肝炎)を呈した高齢透析患者の1例
abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) reactivation in individuals with resolved infection (HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc-positive) usually occurs following immunosuppressive or cytotoxic therapy and may result in severe or fatal hepatitis, whereas spontaneous reactivation without an apparent trigger is uncommon. Here I describe case of a man in his 80s on maintenance dialysis who developed de novo hepatitis B despite no history of immunosuppressive therapy or chemotherapy. Three years before onset, serology revealed HBsAg negativity and isolated anti-HBc positivity. One year before onset, HBV DNA was detected at a low level, and the patient subsequently developed HBeAg-positive hepatitis. In 12 reported cases of spontaneousl development of de novo hepatitis, chronological changes in HBV markers, including HBeAg reverse seroconversion, early HBsAg seroclearrance, and subsequent HBeAg seroconversion. This case emphasizes that HBV reactivation may occur spontaneously during the natural course in elderly patients, possibly because of immune senescence and comorbid conditions, and that dialysis patients may represent a susceptible population. In regions with a high prevalence of prior HBV infection, spontaneous reactivation should be considered as differential diagnosis of new hepatic dysfunction in anti-HBc-positive patients. Careful monitoring of liver function and HBV markers, together with prompt antiviral intervention, when appropriate, is essential for optimal management.

title: Evaluation of Anti-Bacterial and Anti-Cancer Activity of Graphene Oxide-Loaded Magnetic Nanocomposites
abstract: Hepatitis B remains a significant global health concern and dental surgery is considered a potential risk factor for its transmission. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of hepatitis B and its diagnostic associations among participants with a history of dental surgery. HBsAg immuno-chromatic test, qPCR, blood count, LFTs, RFTs, blood sugar, serum electrolytes, and lipid profile were evaluated. Questionnaire was used to collect information on risk factors. The prevalence of HBsAg was 2.9% and HBV DNA was detected among 0.45% of the total participants. A significant association of increasing age (p = 0.0043, R2 = 0.5948) and the number of dental surgeries (p<0.0001) was found with HBsAg prevalence. Appendicitis, blood transfusion, tuberculosis history, cut from the barber/beautician, hospitalization history, and employment status were significant risk factors at p<0.0001. Various diagnostic parameters, such as elevated WBCs, platelets, ALT levels, total bilirubin, low urea, creatinine, cholesterol, serum sodium, and calcium levels were also positively associated (p<0.0001) with HBsAg. Blood group AB+ had the highest HBsAg (6.38%) prevalence. Our findings emphasize the multifactorial nature of hepatitis B transmission and underscore the importance of thorough screening and risk assessment, particularly in individuals with a history of dental surgery. Implementing preventive measures and raising awareness about potential risk factors are important for mitigating the impact of hepatitis B on global health.

This study aimed to assess the prevalence of hepatitis B and its diagnostic associations among participants with a history of dental surgery. HBsAg immuno-chromatic test, qPCR, blood count, LFTs, RFTs, blood sugar, serum electrolytes, and lipid profile were evaluated. Questionnaire was used to collect information on risk factors. The prevalence of HBsAg was 2.9% and HBV DNA was detected among 0.45% of the total participants. A significant association of increasing age (p = 0.0043, R2 = 0.5948) and the number of dental surgeries (p<0.0001) was found with HBsAg prevalence. Appendicitis, blood transfusion, tuberculosis history, cut from the barber/beautician, hospitalization history, and employment status were significant risk factors at p<0.0001. Various diagnostic parameters, such as elevated WBCs, platelets, ALT levels, total bilirubin, low urea, creatinine, cholesterol, serum sodium, and calcium levels were also positively associated (p<0.0001) with HBsAg. Blood group AB+ had the highest HBsAg (6.38%) prevalence. Our findings emphasize the multifactorial nature of hepatitis B transmission and underscore the importance of thorough screening and risk assessment, particularly in individuals with a history of dental surgery. Implementing preventive measures and raising awareness about potential risk factors are important for mitigating the impact of hepatitis B on global health.

title: Hepatitis C virus serological and molecular status and circulating Th1-, Th2- and regulatory cytokines among young adults in Etsako, Edo State, Nigeria: a community-based cross-sectional study
abstract: Abstract Background Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection frequently persists without overt clinical manifestations and can progress silently to chronic liver injury. Anti-HCV immunoglobulin G (IgG) identifies serological exposure but cannot on its own distinguish active from resolved infection, whereas HCV RNA indicates detectable viral genetic material at the time of testing. This study determined anti-HCV IgG and HCV RNA positivity, and examined circulating interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), interleukin-5 (IL-5) and interleukin-10 (IL-10), among young adults in Etsako, Edo State, Nigeria. Methods This community-based cross-sectional study enrolled 200 adults aged 18–35 years (100 women, 100 men) recruited through a multistage household approach between January and June 2023. Venous blood was assayed for anti-HCV IgG, HCV RNA and the three cytokines. Categorical variables were summarised as frequencies and percentages with 95% confidence intervals; cytokine concentrations were summarised as mean ± standard deviation and compared with Welch's unequal-variance t-test, with two-sided P

title: Virus Safety of Blood and Plasma Products: From Established Threats to Emerging Uncertainties
abstract: Following virus transmissions associated with plasma-derived medicinal products (PDMPs) particularly in the 1980s and 1990s, product safety was substantially improved through the “Safety Tripod”: deferral of higher risk donors, testing of plasma for infectious disease markers, and, quantitatively most importantly, pathogen removal and inactivation steps within their industrial manufacturing processes. As a result, virus transmissions by PDMPs have not been reported for many years, including emerging viruses not even tested for. Blood components for transfusion also rely on donor deferral and donation testing, but unlike PDMPs they do not enjoy a manufacturing process that provides for robust virus reduction. Although sensitive nucleic acid tests have reduced HIV, HBV, and HCV transmission risks to below one in a million, additional screening has been required for emerging or newly recognized viruses such as West Nile virus or hepatitis E virus, yet transfusion-transmitted infections still occur. Advances in virology now indicate that known viruses represent only a small fraction of those in circulation, some of which may pose risks after long incubation periods or in immunocompromised patients. As medical progress, particularly in oncology, increases the population of immune-deficient individuals, more dependable blood and plasma safety margins are needed. Implementing virus reduction across PDMPs and blood components represents a science-based, economically reasonable strategy that should inform future regulatory requirements.

title: A novel highly specific qPCR assay for distinguishing HBV cccDNA from rcDNA following bisulfite pretreatment
abstract: ABSTRACT The persistence of covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) underlies chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and remains as the major barrier to achieving a functional cure. An accurate and sensitive quantification of cccDNA is critical for evaluating therapeutic strategies. The conventional quantitative PCR (qPCR) lacks specificity to distinguish cccDNA from viral relaxed circular DNA (rcDNA) and other replicative intermediates, while nuclease pretreatment (e.g., plasmid-safe ATP-dependent nuclease, exonucleases I/III, or T5 exonuclease) may either incompletely digest rcDNA and/or risk over-digesting cccDNA. Here, we evaluated a novel patented bisulfite conversion-based cccDNA (BSC-cccDNA) qPCR platform that employs bisulfite treatment to disrupt rcDNA complementarity, followed by qPCR with primer sets targeting the rcDNA gap region, to enable selective amplification of cccDNA. Using synthetic HBV DNA controls and DNA samples extracted from HBV stable cell line and HBV-infected cells, we demonstrate that the BSC-cccDNA qPCR assay achieves high specificity, with tolerance of up to 10 9 rcDNA copies and sensitivity to 10 cccDNA copies per reaction. Comparative analyses with sensitive digital PCR (dPCR), cross-gap qPCR, and Southern blot further validated the sensitivity and accuracy of the BSC-cccDNA assay. These findings establish the BSC-cccDNA qPCR assay as a reliable tool for standardized cccDNA measurement and highlight its potential for both basic research and clinical applications. IMPORTANCE Accurate quantification of hepatitis B virus (HBV) covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) is critical for understanding viral persistence and evaluating curative therapeutic strategies. However, current PCR-based assays lack sufficient specificity to distinguish cccDNA from relaxed circular DNA (rcDNA). Enzymatic pretreatment approaches to remove rcDNA introduce variability, risk incomplete digestion, and potential cccDNA loss, thereby compromising quantitative accuracy. We evaluated a novel bisulfite conversion-based cccDNA (BSC-cccDNA) qPCR assay that chemically disrupts rcDNA complementarity, enabling highly specific cross-gap amplification without reliance on nuclease digestion. Using synthetic substrates, cell-derived HBV DNA, and infected hepatocyte models, we demonstrate that this assay tolerates up to 109 rcDNA copies while detecting as few as 10 cccDNA copies, with performance validated against Southern blot and dPCR. By improving both specificity and quantitative reliability, the BSC-cccDNA platform provides a potential standardized tool for accurate cccDNA measurement in basic research and therapeutic development.

title: Editorial: Secondary antibody deficiency
abstract: To date, research and attention in the field of immune deficiency has primarily focussed on inborn errors of immunity, driven by their distinct genetic nature which acts as nature's knockout model for understanding human immunology. In contrast, secondary antibody deficiencies often have multifactorial causes and can be much more variable. For example, in a patient with cancer, the antibody deficiency could have multiple contributing factors, including the underlying malignancy, chemotherapy or immunotherapy, radiotherapy, and poor nutritional status. Additionally, there is no well-developed, unified classification system for them, with such patients often being seen by multiple disparate specialties.Nevertheless, secondary antibody deficiencies are of a magnitude greater in frequency compared to inborn errors of immunity, and contribute to significantly larger morbidity and mortality in the population. Their frequency has been increasing rapidly in recent years, with the more widespread use of biologics, immunotherapeutic agents, chemotherapies, and other treatment options for cancers and autoimmune diseases. Because of these advances in therapy, patients are now living longer with disease in remission or under control, but often with a significant compromise to their immune system. Treatments such as CAR-T cell therapy and bispecifics are becoming more common in the management of haematological malignancy, but often carry a profound and long-lasting immunosuppressive effect. The array of immunosuppressive therapies is also increasing rapidly in autoimmune and neurological disease. Further experimental therapies such as trispecifics and BTK degraders are in the pipeline as well.The above factors make raising awareness and better understanding of how to diagnose and treat secondary antibody deficiency even more pertinent. First, there is the issue of recognition and diagnosis of secondary antibody deficiency. Despite the widespread knowledge that certain medications and health conditions can cause secondary antibody deficiency, it is unfortunately not infrequent that appropriate screening is not undertaken. In their article, Elkhalifa et al. discuss the need for greater awareness of the importance of monitoring for secondary antibody deficiency in patients susceptible to it, and propose ways to identify them. 1 In the same direction, Lagnese et al. propose a diagnostic algorithm that may be used regardless of the underlying aetiology in these patients. 2 They also discuss the need for further research into predicting the likelihood of secondary antibody deficiency, as well as into which of patients will become susceptible to infection.Even when secondary antibody deficiency is recognised, management is not always appropriate, with both unnecessarily delayed and over-zealous treatment occurring in practice. There are various contributory factors to this, including the variable training received and experience in secondary antibody deficiency among different specialties that will see these patients, as well as the lack of universally accepted guidelines on how to manage them. In this manner, Elkhalifa et al summarise potential treatment strategies for these patients, as recommended by the various national and international guidelines. offer another perspective into the management algorithms for these patients. 2 Immunoglobulin therapy, which is a key treatment for secondary antibody deficiency, remains in limited supply and hence it is vital to determine which patients will benefit the most from it. Some more nuanced points within this research topic are that there can be an overlap between primary and secondary immune deficiency, as exemplified in the case report by Johnston et al. 3 In this, a patient who presented with recurrent lower respiratory tract infections and borderline hypogammaglobulinaemia is described. The patient was initially diagnosed with anticonvulsantinduced secondary antibody deficiency, but on further evaluation the diagnosis was changed to RNU4ATAC-associated Roifman syndrome. This case highlights the importance of keeping an open mind when evaluating patients with immunodeficiency, and of not hesitating to review the diagnosis in them.Finally, the article by Luo et al focuses on the infectious complications that can be seen in patients with secondary antibody deficiency. 4 They present a case of hepatitis B virus reactivation following rituximab therapy in a patient receiving maintenance hemodialysis. This case highlights the importance of keeping a high index of suspicion for infections in these patients, and of the importance of using appropriate screening methods.In conclusion, it is important to emphasize that secondary antibody deficiency needs to be viewed as a predictable and manageable complication of the modern therapies that we have, rather than as a delayed afterthought. Although secondary antibody deficiency is gaining greater prominence, there is still much work to be done to improve the care of patients affected by it. It is also important that we improve training and develop universally accepted management protocols for these patients. As the number of therapies that suppress the immune system continues to rise, it is critical that their use begins to incorporate protection of the immune function as part of their standard delivery package.

title: Analysis of Genetic Characteristics of Hepatitis C Virus among Sentinel Surveillance Populations in Fujian Province, China from 2022 to 2025
abstract: Abstract Objective To analyze the genotype distribution, evolution, and characteristics of resistance-associated substitutions (RASs) of Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) among sentinel surveillance populations in Fujian Province from 2022 to 2025, and to provide a scientific basis for HCV prevention and control. Methods The hepatitis C incidence report data from 2022 to 2025 in Fujian Province were obtained from the China CDC Information System. Full-length HCV genome sequences were obtained through high-throughput sequencing, and bioinformatics software was employed to analyze genetic characteristics and RAS distribution. Results From 2022 to 2025, sentinel surveillance in Fujian Province revealed that HCV infections were predominantly subtype 1b, with escalating trends observed in subtypes 3b and 6a. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that most 1b, 3b, and 6a sequences clustered closely with Guangdong Province sequences, while some lineages also grouped with international sequences from Japan and Denmark. Sequences of subtypes 1a and 2a were more likely to cluster with international sequences. In the HCV NS3/4A region, resistance-associated substitutions (RASs) S122G/N/C occurred most frequently in subtypes 1b and 6a (31/91). In the NS5A region, RASs conferring higher drug resistance included L31V and Y93H, R30Q and L28M in subtype 1b, and Q30K+L31M in subtype 3b. In the NS5B region, RASs-C316N was predominantly detected in subtype 1b (21/32), and when coexisting with S556G, it conferred higher resistance to DSV. Concurrent presence of RASs in both NS5B and NS5A regions reduced SOF treatment efficacy. Conclusions The genetic distribution of sentinel populations in Fujian Province tends to be increasingly complex. Population mobility and overseas importation are important factors in virus transmission. Drug resistance-related substitution mutations are commonly present in sentinel populations, and using whole-genome sequencing to track drug resistance mutations generated by genetic diversity in epidemic strains is very important for accurately guiding treatment of hepatitis C patients.

source_records.title: Analysis of Genetic Characteristics of Hepatitis C Virus among Sentinel Surveillance Populations in Fujian Province, China from 2022 to 2025
source_records.abstract: Abstract Objective To analyze the genotype distribution, evolution, and characteristics of resistance-associated substitutions (RASs) of Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) among sentinel surveillance populations in Fujian Province from 2022 to 2025, and to provide a scientific basis for HCV prevention and control. Methods The hepatitis C incidence report data from 2022 to 2025 in Fujian Province were obtained from the China CDC Information System. Full-length HCV genome sequences were obtained through high-throughput sequencing, and bioinformatics software was employed to analyze genetic characteristics and RAS distribution. Results From 2022 to 2025, sentinel surveillance in Fujian Province revealed that HCV infections were predominantly subtype 1b, with escalating trends observed in subtypes 3b and 6a. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated that most 1b, 3b, and 6a sequences clustered closely with Guangdong Province sequences, while some lineages also grouped with international sequences from Japan and Denmark. Sequences of subtypes 1a and 2a were more likely to cluster with international sequences. In the HCV NS3/4A region, resistance-associated substitutions (RASs) S122G/N/C occurred most frequently in subtypes 1b and 6a (31/91). In the NS5A region, RASs conferring higher drug resistance included L31V and Y93H, R30Q and L28M in subtype 1b, and Q30K+L31M in subtype 3b. In the NS5B region, RASs-C316N was predominantly detected in subtype 1b (21/32), and when coexisting with S556G, it conferred higher resistance to DSV. Concurrent presence of RASs in both NS5B and NS5A regions reduced SOF treatment efficacy. Conclusions The genetic distribution of sentinel populations in Fujian Province tends to be increasingly complex. Population mobility and overseas importation are important factors in virus transmission. Drug resistance-related substitution mutations are commonly present in sentinel populations, and using whole-genome sequencing to track drug resistance mutations generated by genetic diversity in epidemic strains is very important for accurately guiding treatment of hepatitis C patients.

title: Safer smoking supply distribution as a harm reduction strategy for people who smoke drugs in New York State: A qualitative analysis of availability, utilization, and public health impact
abstract: Abstract Background The U.S. overdose crisis and communicable diseases such as hepatitis C virus continue to disproportionately affect people who use drugs (PWUD), amid a shift from injection to smoking fentanyl and other unregulated substances. Syringe exchange programs (SEPs) have expanded to include safer smoking supply distribution as a harm reduction strategy to reduce equipment sharing, prevent injury and infectious disease transmission, and strengthen engagement among people who smoke drugs. The NYS Department of Health (NYSDOH) Office of Drug User Health (ODUH) oversees 41 Syringe Exchange Programs (SEPs) and 12 Drug User Health Hubs within them, delivering safer use supplies and other comprehensive services for underserved populations. Despite expanding implementation, evidence on availability, utilization, and public health impact in NYS remains limited. Objectives To examine the availability and utilization of safer smoking supplies in NYS and their public health benefits for PWUD. Methods We conducted semi-structured interviews with 30 conveniently sampled PWUD from 10 harm reduction organizations across NYS. Sites were selected based on supply distribution, geographic diversity, and for one site, age. Applied thematic analysis and consensus coding were conducted using Dedoose, guided by the RE-AIM framework to assess program reach and effectiveness. Participants received a $35 Visa gift card upon completion. Results Participants expressed how safer smoking supply distribution facilitated engagement with public health services including wound care, mental health support, and substance use treatment. Access to supplies was consistently linked to increased harm reduction services utilization. While participants identified ongoing funding gaps, most reported regular access to supplies such as pipes, mouthpieces, screens, foil and hygiene materials. Programs also extended critical supports including housing assistance, food access and navigation of complex healthcare systems. Conclusion Harm reduction minimizes the adverse health, social, and legal consequences of drug use without requiring abstinence. Safer smoking supply distribution enhances engagement by creating consistent, low-barrier points of contact and often serves as a critical entryway to care. In NYS, these programs function as essential infrastructure, connecting underserved populations to health services and advancing more equitable public health outcomes.

title: A cross-sectional study on knowledge and practice of caregivers of under-5 children regarding EPI
abstract: Background: The Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) is one of the most successful and cost effective public health interventions for vaccine-preventable diseases of under-5 children in Bangladesh. Complete and timely immunization of under-5 children largely depends upon the knowledge and practice of caregivers’ regarding vaccination. Evaluating caregivers’ knowledge and practices regarding EPI is necessary to find out the gaps and enhance immunization services. Objective: To assess the knowledge and practice of caregivers of under-5 children regarding EPI at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital & Institute, Dhaka. Methods: It was a descriptive cross-sectional study conducted from 8th to 22nd February 2025 among caregivers of under-5 children attending the outpatient department (OPD) and EPI centre of Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, Dhaka. The knowledge and practice of the caregivers regarding EPI were assessed using 8 questions on knowledge and 5 on practice, assigning a score of 1 for each correct response and 0 for each incorrect response. Purposive sampling technique was used for data collection and the final sample size was 148. The data were analysed via SPSS (version 31.0). Results: The mean age of the under-5 children was 16.12±12.37 months (mean±SD) and the majority (53.4%) of under-5 children were aged 0-12 months. The study population included 50.7% males and 49.3% females. The majority were Muslim (72.3%) and resided in urban areas (70.3%). More than three-fifths (62.2%) of the caregivers reported health centres as their source of knowledge about EPI. Three-fourths (75%) of the participants had adequate knowledge, while the majority (95.3%) demonstrated good practices regarding EPI. Conclusion: The results of our study revealed that the majority of the participants had an adequate level of knowledge and demonstrated good practice regarding immunization of under-5 children. The majority first heard about vaccination from health centres and were aware that tuberculosis, measles, rubella, polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus and hepatitis B can be prevented by vaccine. However, most of the participants lacked knowledge that vaccine can prevent diseases like meningitis and pneumonia also. DS (Child) H J 2025; 41(1): 31-35

title: Integrated biomarkers and renal Doppler for early acute kidney injury diagnosis in hepatitis C virus cirrhosis
abstract: BACKGROUND Acute kidney injury (AKI) complicates up to 65% of hospitalizations for decompensated cirrhosis and is associated with high short-term mortality. Traditional markers such as serum creatinine are unreliable in cirrhosis, while novel biomarkers like neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), cystatin C, and Doppler renal resistive index (RRI) show promise but have not been systematically validated in hepatitis C virus-endemic, resource-limited settings such as Egypt. AIM To evaluate the diagnostic and prognostic utility of NGAL, cystatin C, and RRI for early AKI detection, subtyping [pre-renal, hepatorenal syndrome (HRS), acute tubular necrosis (ATN)], and mortality risk stratification in cirrhotic patients. METHODS In this prospective cohort study, 120 cirrhotic patients with ascites were enrolled and categorized into three groups: Non-AKI (n = 42), pre-renal AKI (n = 43), and intrinsic AKI (n = 35), the latter subdivided into HRS (n = 20) and ATN (n = 15). Serum NGAL and cystatin C were quantified using commercially available enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kits; RRI was obtained via standardized Doppler ultrasonography. AKI was staged per International Club of Ascites-Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes guidelines. To reflect real-world presentation, the cohort included both prevalent (present at admission) and incident (developing postadmission) AKI cases. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, and Cox regression models evaluated 30-day mortality. An NGAL-RRI-based machine-learning model (XGBoost) was developed for AKI subtyping, and a decision-tree model was constructed. Point-of-care ultrasound was associated with the reclassification of 42% of diagnostically ambiguous AKI cases. RESULTS AKI was present in 65% (78/120) of patients. Of these, 52 (66.7%) had AKI at admission, and 26 (33.3%) developed AKI during hospitalization. NGAL distinguished AKI with area under the curve (AUC) of 0.91 (95%CI: 0.87-0.95) [cutoff > 150 ng/mL, sensitivity of 90% (85%-94%), specificity of 85% (78%-90%)]. RRI > 0.74 identified HRS with AUC of 0.89 (95%CI: 0.83-0.94) with sensitivity of 82%, specificity of 88%. Cystatin C showed moderate diagnostic value [AUC of 0.86 (95%CI: 0.81-0.91)]. Urinary granular casts were specific for ATN (100%), while renin and aldosterone levels were highest in HRS. NGAL > 150 ng/mL was independently associated with higher 30-day mortality (hazard ratio = 3.1, 95%CI: 1.7-5.5), while RRI > 0.74 was associated with poor renal recovery (hazard ratio = 2.2, P = 0.003). The internally validated NGAL-RRI XGBoost model achieved a cross-validated AUC of 0.92 for AKI subtyping. Excluding borderline fractional excretion of sodium cases improved HRS AUC from 0.91 to 0.93. Implementation of an NGAL-guided triage protocol corresponded to a 28% lower rate of intensive care unit transfers in a simulated decision framework (14/50 avoided). CONCLUSION NGAL and RRI outperform creatinine in early AKI detection, subtyping, and prognostication in cirrhotic patients, while cystatin C adds diagnostic value, particularly in ambiguous cases. An NGAL-RRI-based algorithm, enhanced by cystatin C when needed, represents a practical, resource-efficient tool for AKI triage in resource-limited settings.

title: A capsid hinge region in European hepatitis E virus links mutations to genotype, virion surface properties, and environmental circulation
abstract: ABSTRACT Hepatitis E virus (HEV) exhibits genetic diversity associated with distinct public health outcomes and circulation patterns across interconnected human and environmental reservoirs. Most studies have focused on genome-wide diversity, revealing relationships between genotype, virulence, and dissemination routes. However, the role of localized mutations in the capsid protein (ORF2), which may influence the extracellular fate and ecology of HEV through changes in surface biological and physicochemical properties of virions, received limited attention. Here, we combined large-scale analysis of European HEV sequences, structural modeling, and physicochemical characterization to investigate such variations in ORF2. Analysis of ORF2 sequences on a genomic segment highly reported in GenBank, derived from patients and the environment, revealed recurrent mutation motifs (single H354Y and triple H354Y–G357S–V364I motifs) located in a conserved capsid hinge region connecting the middle (M) and protruding (P) domains of the protein. These motifs displayed distinct frequency patterns according to sequence sources and were associated with genotypes 3 and 1, respectively. AlphaFold-based modeling identified this region as a flexible interface between the M and P domains and indicated that mutations reduce predicted alignment error of the P domain relative to the overall protein model, consistent with altered exposure at the virion surface. In vitro analyses of synthetic peptides encompassing this critical region revealed increased hydrophobicity and structural rearrangements, supporting local modulation of capsid surface properties. Together, these results identify a structurally and physicochemically sensitive hinge region in the HEV capsid, suggesting a link between ORF2 sequence variations, genotype, virion surface properties, and environmental circulation. IMPORTANCE Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a major cause of viral hepatitis worldwide, which is transmitted through complex, genotype-linked dissemination routes between humans, animals, and environmental waters. Understanding the circulation dynamics of HEV virions is essential for improving environmental surveillance, risk assessment, and public health strategies within a One Health approach. By combining genetic, structural, and physicochemical analyses, this study highlights specific mutation motifs in a hinge region of the ORF2 capsid protein likely to link distinct distribution patterns of HEV across environmental reservoirs to potential changes in virion surface properties. Such mutation motifs may serve as molecular signatures for exploring virus persistence and dissemination in environmental contexts. Overall, this work provides a new framework for connecting viral genetic variation to environmental behavior beyond traditional genotype classification.

title: A divergent hepatitis A virus lineage in wild western lowland gorillas and central chimpanzees supports localized circulation and expands HAV diversity
abstract: Abstract Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is a ubiquitous human pathogen that may cause acute liver disease. Despite the availability of effective vaccines, high prevalence rates are still reported in Southeast Asia and Africa, where sanitation conditions are poor. Although seven genotypes are known, including three in humans, three in non-human primates (NHP), and one in alpacas, the diversity, ecology, and evolutionary history of HAV remain poorly understood. In a pilot study of virome molecular characterization of wild African apes by using oligonucleotide probes enrichment, HAV sequences were detected in two animals (2/105; 1.9%): one from a western lowland gorilla (G. gorilla) from southern Cameroon, sampled in 2006, and another from a central chimpanzee (P. troglodytes) in northeastern Gabon, sampled in 2011, approximately at 450 km apart. Two near-full-length viral genomes were successfully reconstructed using specific primer sets that were developed. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that these sequences cluster within the simian HAV clade, forming a distinct cluster closely related to environmental strains from the Sanaga River in Cameroon and South Africa, yet clearly divergent from genotype V sequences (≥15.8% nucleotide divergence in the VP1 protein). Amino acid comparisons identified residues conserved in simian HAVs and, subsequently, only in African HAV strains. These results support the classification of a supplementary African simian genotype, provisionally designated HAV-VIII. HAV-positive samples (13/227; 5.7%) were detected in the same field sites, suggesting localized viral circulation in these populations. Bayesian time-scaled phylogenetic analysis estimated the most recent common ancestor of the human and simian HAV lineages at ~2,291 years ago and that of simian lineages at ~1,900 years ago, with a more recent diversification (~100 years ago) within the identified lineage. This study highlights the presence of HAV in wild ape populations for the first time and also the first HAV detection among NHP species in Central Africa. These findings contribute to our current understanding of the diversity and evolution of HAV and highlight the need to extend surveillance across NHP species to better assess potential zoonotic risks.

title: Prevalence and risk factors of current hepatitis C infection among men who have sex with men aged 20-59 years: NHANES 1999-2016.
abstract: Background Men who have sex with men (MSM) are a key population with a higher prevalence of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection than the general population. Our study estimated the prevalence of current HCV infection and identified risk factors among MSM aged 20-59 years in the US from 1999 to 2016. Methods Data were obtained from the 1999-2016 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). Current HCV infection was defined as having a positive HCV RNA test result. The prevalence of current HCV infection was weighted according to the complex survey design of NHANES. A Rao-Scott Chi-squared test was used to compare the differences between HCV-positive and HCV-negative MSM. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify risk factors for current HCV infection. Results In the US, nearly 5.1% (95% CI 4.5-5.7) of the general population self-reported as MSM. The weighted prevalence of current HCV infection was 1.8% (95% CI 1.5-2.1) among non-institutionalized US males, and 3.5% (95% CI 1.9-5.7) among MSM. Current HCV infection among MSM was associated with injection drug use (aOR 29.2, 95% CI 12.1-70.8), blood transfusion (aOR 8.2, 95% CI 1.5-45.7), being aged 40-59 years (aOR 4.0, 95% CI 1.6-10.1) and having a poverty income ratio Conclusions In the US, the prevalence of current HCV infection is nearly twice as high among MSM as among males in the general population, suggesting the need for surveillance of the HCV epidemic among MSM. Prevention and control strategies targeting the risk factors are critical to combating the HCV epidemic among MSM.

title: Maternal and fetal risk factors for hypospadias: a hospital-based case-control study in Southern China
abstract: Hypospadias is a frequent congenital anomaly in male infants, defined by the urethral meatus opening on the ventral surface of the penis. Although its causes have been examined for many years, the underlying aetiology in most affected children remains unclear. Maternal factors such as pre-pregnancy body mass index (BMI), gestational weight gain, BMI at delivery and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) have been suggested as modifiable factors independently associated with hypospadias, yet existing epidemiological studies report mixed and sometimes conflicting results. In this context, the present study aims to systematically evaluate maternal and fetal risk factors for hypospadias to help resolve these uncertainties. From 2019 to 2021, a retrospective hospital-based case-control study was carried out in Hainan, China. Women delivering newborns with hypospadias were enrolled as cases, while women delivering normal newborns were randomly selected as controls. The study included 96 infants with hypospadias and 480 male controls from Hainan Maternal and Child Health Hospital. Maternal demographic and clinical characteristics were extracted from archived clinical records; the relevant information was originally collected via face-to-face or telephone communication as part of routine clinical care. Clinical data pertaining to birth outcomes and maternal complications were verified from medical records. We compared maternal and fetal characteristics between offspring with and without hypospadias. Multivariable conditional logistic regression was performed to identify factors independently associated with hypospadias. No associations of maternal weight before pregnancy, maternal body weight gain during pregnancy, BMI at delivery, maternal age, and Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) infection with hypospadias in offspring were observed. Maternal education (aOR 0.35, 95% CI 0.18-0.68 and aOR 0.18, 95% CI 0.07-0.50), gestational hypertension (aOR 6.27, 95% CI 2.44-16.13), intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (aOR 13.86, 95% CI 3.00-64.03), hypothyroidism (aOR 16.63, 95% CI 5.01- 55.20), birth weight (aOR 19.07, 95% CI 6.58- 55.25) and multiple gestation (aOR 7.89, 95% CI 1.05-59.48) were independently associated with hypospadias in offspring. These findings may help generate hypotheses regarding maternal and fetal characteristics associated with hypospadias and warrant confirmation in larger prospective studies.

title: Immunoinformatics-based design of a multi-epitope mRNA vaccine candidate targeting the major human-infecting hepatitis E virus genotypes 1–4
abstract: Background Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is one of the leading causes of acute and chronic hepatitis among humans across the globe and is linked to severe diseases in immunocompromised individuals and pregnant women. Despite its substantial global burden, only one vaccine is licensed (in China and Pakistan), limiting its global accessibility. Furthermore, no globally approved mRNA vaccine against HEV is currently available, highlighting the need to develop strategies for alternative vaccines. Methods In this study, the amino acid sequences of ORF2 capsid proteins representative of HEV genotypes 1–4 were curated, retrieved, and analyzed to generate a consensus sequence. The conserved cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL), helper T lymphocyte (HTL), and B-cell epitopes were computationally screened based on their antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, IFN-γ induction, and human non-homology. Then, the selected epitopes, seven in total, were assembled into a computational multi-epitope mRNA construct incorporated with β-defensin adjuvant, correct linkers, and regulatory elements [Kozak, tPA, MITD, and globin untranslated regions (UTRs)]. The construct was subsequently subjected to structural modeling, refinement and validation, docked with the TLR1/TLR2 heterodimer, followed by normal mode analysis and a 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation with MM-GBSA binding free-energy estimation, immune simulations, codon optimization, and in silico vaccine construct design. Results The computational analyses predicted that the proposed epitopes possessed a favorable antigenicity (VaxiJen score ≥0.4–1), with non-allergenicity and epitope conservancy (80%–100%) across the analyzed HEV genotypes (1–4), and that the assembled vaccine construct was structurally stable. Protein–protein docking of the vaccine construct candidate with the TLR1/TLR2 heterodimer and normal mode analysis of the docked complex indicated a stable structural interface rather than a confirmation of biological receptor engagement; a subsequent 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation supported a persistent, increasingly hydrogen-bonded interface with a favorable MM-GBSA binding free-energy (−91.96 kcal/mol). Computational immune simulations predicted cellular and humoral immune responses with B- and T-cell interaction activity and cytokine production levels. Conclusion This study describes a computationally designed multi-epitope mRNA vaccine candidate with predicted immunogenicity and structural stability against the major human-infecting HEV genotypes 1–4. These computational results support the proposed vaccine construct as a promising candidate for further research to assess its immunogenicity; safety and protective efficacy will require experimental validation before its translational potential is verified.

title: Hepatitis E Virus Infection in Pregnant Women
abstract: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a major global public health concern, particularly in resource-limited regions. Approximately 12.5% of individuals worldwide have been exposed to HEV, and 15–110 million individuals have current or recent HEV infection. HEV poses an especially serious threat to pregnant women, in whom infection can progress to severe disease and is associated with a high case fatality rate, particularly during the third trimester. Moreover, maternal HEV infection can lead to various adverse outcomes in fetuses and/or neonates, as documented in both developing and developed countries. No HEV-specific antiviral therapy is approved for use during pregnancy, and pregnancy-specific evidence and recommendations for HEV vaccination remain limited. This narrative review summarizes the diagnosis, prevalence, clinical manifestations, mechanisms underlying severe disease, treatment, and prevention of HEV infection in this high-risk population. It aims to improve clinicians’ awareness of the potential impact of HEV infection on pregnant women and their fetuses/neonates, to promote public health literacy, and to accelerate future disease-control efforts.

title: Maternal hepatitis E virus infection: Immunopathogenesis, genotype-specific severity, and vertical transmission dynamics
abstract: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection remains a major global health concern, particularly in regions with poor sanitation and limited access to safe water. Although usually self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals, HEV can cause severe maternal and fetal complications during pregnancy. This review summarizes current evidence on the clinical manifestations, immunopathogenesis, genotype-specific disease patterns, and transmission of HEV in pregnancy. Pregnancy-associated immune modulation, hormonal changes, and placental adaptations promote viral replication and impair antiviral responses, particularly in the later stages of gestation. Disease severity varies by genotype, with human-restricted genotypes 1 and 2 causing the most severe pregnancy outcomes, whereas zoonotic genotypes 3 and 4 generally result in milder disease. source_records.abstract: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection remains a major global health concern, particularly in regions with poor sanitation and limited access to safe water. title: Hepatitis E vaccination in women of childbearing age: safety and tolerability outcomes
abstract: Abstract Background and objective Hepatitis E virus is a major cause of acute viral hepatitis and is endemic in Pakistan, where it contributes substantially to morbidity and mortality among women of childbearing age. The Hecolin vaccine is a potentially useful preventive measure, but data on its safety in this population remain limited. This study assessed the safety and tolerability of hepatitis E vaccination in non-pregnant women of childbearing age. Methodology This prospective, multicenter observational study was conducted at Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre and Atiya General Hospital, Karachi, Pakistan, from September 2023 to September 2025. Using non-probability convenience sampling, 375 non-pregnant women aged 16–43 years, stratified into 16–22 and 23–43-year subgroups, received at least one vaccine dose and were followed for 21 days. Data were collected by structured questionnaire and analyzed with descriptive statistics and the Chi-square test, with p ≤ 0.05 considered significant. Results Among the 375 non-pregnant women (mean age 24.47 ± 5.44 years), 72 (19.2%) were married and 303 (80.8%) unmarried; occupations included students (39.5%), housewives (24.8%), caretakers (14.7%), teachers (6.9%), office workers (5.6%), laborers (5.3%), and doctors (3.2%), and 369 (98.4%) resided in Sindh. Adverse effects were mild, transient, and most frequent after the first dose fever (3.7%), flu-like symptoms (4.8%), headache (1.9%), and cold sores (0.3%) all declining on subsequent follow-ups, with no serious adverse events and similar tolerability across age groups. Conclusion Hepatitis E vaccination is safe, well-tolerated, and acceptable in non-pregnant women of reproductive age in endemic settings, supporting its inclusion in public health programs to reduce hepatitis E-related morbidity and mortality. Further studies should assess long-term protection and safety in pregnancy.

title: Antiviral Sesquiterpene Lactones from Laurus nobilis L.: Inhibition of Hepatitis C Virus and Dengue Virus Replication
abstract: Natural products remain indispensable scaffolds in antiviral drug discovery, particularly against high-burden viral pathogens. In this study, two major sesquiterpene lactones, dehydrocostus lactone (1) and costunolide (2), were isolated from Laurus nobilis L. leaves and evaluated for their antiviral potential against hepatitis C virus (HCV) and dengue virus (DENV). The structures of both compounds were confirmed by HRMS and 1D NMR spectroscopic analyses. In subgenomic replicon assays, the molecules inhibited HCV replication in the low-micromolar range (EC50=2.34 μM for 1 and 2.06 μM for 2) with favorable selectivity indices. In full-length HCV reporter systems, costunolide (2) displayed enhanced anti-HCV potency, reduced viral RNA and NS5A protein levels, and enhanced the suppressive effect of the clinically approved NS5A inhibitor, daclatasvir. Furthermore, costunolide (2) exhibited cross-flaviviridae activity, suppressing DENV replication (EC50=5.89 μM in replicon cells; EC50=1.27 μM post-infection in infectious virus assays), and demonstrated cooperative suppression of viral propagation along with reduced glutathione. Mechanistically, these results highlight the critical role of the sesquiterpene lactone core, and the observed enhanced combined activity between costunolide and reduced glutathione is consistent with a possible contribution of the NRF2/glutathione antioxidant axis to its anti-DENV action. Overall, this study highlights L. nobilis as a previously underexplored source of antiviral sesquiterpene lactones and establishes costunolide (2) as a promising lead against HCV and DENV, warranting further investigation across additional Flaviviridae members.
